title: Caching
oneLiner: Keep a copy of hot data somewhere fast, and decide how stale that copy is allowed to get.
keyTakeaway: A cache works because real traffic is skewed: a small set of hot keys gets most of the reads, so a cache much smaller than the database can absorb most of the load. The cost is staleness, so every cache needs an answer to "what happens when the data changes": a TTL, deleting on write, or both.
explanation:
A cache is a faster, smaller copy of data that lives closer to whoever needs it. Caches exist at every layer: the browser keeps images and scripts, a CDN (content delivery network, servers spread around the world) keeps static files in a city near the user, the application keeps objects in its own memory, a shared cache like Redis or Memcached (in-memory key-value stores) keeps query results for every app server, and the database itself keeps hot pages in its buffer pool so it can skip the disk. In an interview, "add a cache" is only half an answer; say which layer, what goes in it, and how it gets invalidated.

The most common pattern is cache-aside: the app checks the cache, and on a miss it reads the database and puts the result in the cache for next time. The cache only ever holds data someone asked for, and if the cache dies the app still works, just slower. Write-through writes to the cache and the database together on every update, so reads are always fresh but every write pays for both. Write-back (write-behind) writes only to the cache and flushes to the database later, which makes writes very fast but loses data if the cache dies before the flush.

Part 1 shows why caches work at all. With a DB read at 50 ms and a cache hit at 1 ms, the average latency is set almost entirely by the hit rate: 90% hits gives about 6 ms, 50% hits about 26 ms. Set the skew to 0 and every key is equally popular, so a cache holding a sixth of the keys hits about a sixth of the time. Raise the skew to something like real traffic and a small cache hits most of the time. The database load drops by the same factor, which is often the real reason to add the cache.

When the cache is full, the eviction policy picks what to throw out. LRU (least recently used) is the usual default and works well when recent use predicts future use. LFU (least frequently used) keeps the steady favorites even through a burst of one-off keys. Random eviction is cheap and surprisingly close for small caches, but it sometimes evicts a hot key. A TTL (time to live) is the other way entries leave: after a fixed time the entry expires and the next read goes to the database.

There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things. Part 2 shows why. If nothing tells the cache that the data changed, readers get the old value until the TTL runs out, so the TTL is your bound on staleness. Deleting the key on every write fixes the common case; delete rather than overwrite, because two concurrent writers updating the cache can leave the older value behind. Even then there are small race windows, which is why most systems keep a TTL as a safety net.

Part 3 is the cache stampede, or thundering herd. A hot key expires and hundreds of requests miss at the same moment, all asking the database for the same row. The fix is request coalescing: the first miss loads the value while the rest wait for it. Adding random jitter to TTLs and refreshing hot keys shortly before they expire help too.

Not everything should be cached. Data that must be exactly current (an account balance before a payment, stock levels at checkout) should be read from the source of truth. Data that is rarely read twice wastes cache space. Per-user private data in a shared cache needs a key that includes the user, or one user sees another's page. And a cache is not a database: anything stored only in the cache can disappear at any time.
